status_reasoning: Reviewers challenge the claim that Notch functions independently of cell fate, stating 'this is far from being demonstrated as only two molecular markers are shown to be identical (Acj6 and Ato)' and noting 'it is highly likely that the two cell populations are different from one another since they project differently, target different neurons, and might have different neurotransmitters.' They request discussion of whether 'there are not in fact two subsets of DCN neurons and that Notch functions classically in fate determination.'

Reviewers affirm the main finding, stating 'This is an interesting finding, which is globally well supported by the data, and which reveals a novel non-deterministic strategy by which reproducible nervous system connectivity is achieved.' They acknowledge the mechanism shows 'a re-utilization of the same pathway used in lateral inhibition' and that the data demonstrates 'only a fixed number of neurons, inversely proportional to the size of the cluster, choose to target the medulla rather than the lobula.'

Reviewers note 'it is unclear where Notch functions and this could be clarified either with new data or at least in the Discussion. Is the Delta/Notch signaling functioning in the axons themselves (is Notch detectable in this compartment), or within the soma as implied indirectly by the relationship established early in the manuscript between DCN soma clustering and axonal target choice?' This indicates uncertainty about the subcellular location of Notch function.

While reviewers comment that 'The modeling is nice and does not detract from the quality of the paper' and note 'it is not necessary to use equations to predict that loss of Notch will lead to an increase in the proportion of medulla projecting neurons,' they do not challenge the validity of the computational predictions themselves. The critique is about necessity rather than accuracy, implying acceptance of the modeling results.

Reviewers raise concerns about Figure 8 data presentation, noting 'Figure 8h, it would be more illustrative to show an example in which a similar number of axons are labelled with GFP as in Figure 8i' to better demonstrate the effect. They also question 'Figure 8i shows a cluster of one mutant (green) and one wild-type (red) axon, which is counter to their model that wild type axons compensate for the presence of mutant axons by restricting to the lobula – what is the explanation for this?' This suggests uncertainty about the interpretation of multi-cell clone data.

Reviewers request that 'Figure 8k: the distances between adjacent axons should be calculated for all axons and not only for GFP positive axons,' suggesting the current analysis may be incomplete or potentially biased. This indicates uncertainty about whether the spacing measurements fully support the compensatory mechanism in single-cell clones.

Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the quantitative findings, stating 'Very careful quantification of the projections and cell bodies indicates that there is extensive variability in the number of DCN produced from the unique neuroblast, as well as variability in the number of clusters along the dorso-ventral axis, but surprisingly a light level of stereotypy in the total number of neurons that project to the medulla.' This affirms the core anatomical observations.

Reviewers accept the genetic manipulation data showing Notch pathway involvement, as evidenced by their statement that the finding 'is globally well supported by the data.' They do not challenge the loss-of-function experiments showing increased medulla axons or clustered axon phenotypes, instead focusing their concerns on interpretation regarding cell fate independence.

Reviewers acknowledge the temporal requirement for Notch, noting 'The authors address when Notch is required' without challenging the temporal window findings. Their concern is about 'where Notch functions' rather than when, indicating acceptance of the timing data showing Notch acts during 24-60 hr APF.

Reviewers do not challenge the single-cell MARCM data showing cell-autonomous effects and probabilistic targeting. Their acceptance is implicit in their focus on interpretation (fate vs. non-fate) rather than questioning the experimental observations themselves. The probabilistic nature (~60% medulla targeting in mutants vs ~24% in controls) aligns with the reviewers' acknowledgment of the 'non-deterministic strategy.'
